Contradict

/kon-truh-DIKT/ · verb

Hear It

What It Means

Contradict means to assert the opposite of a statement, or to be inconsistent with it.

New sailors quickly learn that it is risky to contradict the captain on deck.

Worked Example

The intern chose not to contradict the senior engineer, even though the blueprints clearly showed a different measurement.

To contradict the engineer would be to state, out loud, the opposite of what he said. The infinitive 'to contradict' shows the act being weighed as a choice — one the intern decides against.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

gainsay: to deny or dispute (formal)

negate: to deny; to cancel out

rebut: to argue against with evidence

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

affirm: to state firmly as true

uphold: to support or confirm

Where it sits · how decisively a claim is opposed — question → contradict → refute

question vs. contradict: To question a statement is only to ask whether it is true; to contradict it is to assert the opposite outright.

refute vs. contradict: To contradict a claim is to declare it wrong; to refute it is to prove it wrong.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — contra-

Prefix — contra-: against, opposite (Latin)

Root — dict

Root — dict: to say, to speak (Latin dicere)

Put it together

Put it together: Contra- ('against') plus dict- ('to say'): to contradict is literally to 'speak against' what someone else has said.

Use the root in a new word: diction

Use the root in a new word: diction: The actor's crisp diction made every word of the speech easy to hear — diction is your manner of saying words.

Root Check

Word Choice

Neutral / formal

Contradict takes a direct object — you contradict someone or something — unlike disagree, which needs 'with.' Contradicting a person to their face is blunter and more confrontational than merely disagreeing with them, which is why so many sentences pair it with hesitation: 'didn't dare to contradict,' 'was reluctant to contradict.'
